name: Apple scab
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves that turn dark and scabby; leaves may yellow and fall early, and fruit gets rough scabs.
treatment: Collect and destroy fallen leaves. Prune to open the tree canopy for air and sunlight. Spray a recommended fungicide such as captan, mancozeb or sulphur from green-tip to petal fall, as advised locally.
prevention: Grow scab-resistant varieties, clear leaf litter every autumn, and avoid overhead irrigation.

name: Apple black rot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Brown leaf spots with a purple edge (frogeye), rotting fruit with black rings, and sunken cankers on branches.
treatment: Prune out cankers and dead wood and burn them. Remove rotten and dried fruit. Spray a recommended fungicide as per label and local advice.
prevention: Keep the orchard clean, avoid wounding the bark, and keep trees well fed and watered.

name: Cedar apple rust
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface with small tube-like growths underneath. The disease needs nearby juniper or cedar trees.
treatment: Remove nearby juniper or cedar galls if possible. Spray a recommended fungicide such as myclobutanil or mancozeb from the pink-bud stage, following the label.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties and keep apple trees away from juniper and cedar.

name: Cherry powdery mildew
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: White powdery growth on leaves, which curl, twist and become distorted. Young shoots are most affected.
treatment: Prune and destroy infected shoots. Improve air flow. Spray sulphur or another recommended fungicide at the first signs, following the label.
prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen, do not overcrowd trees, and choose tolerant varieties.

name: Maize gray leaf spot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Narrow rectangular tan to gray spots running along the leaf veins. In humid weather the spots join and leaves dry up.
treatment: Remove or bury crop residue. If spots reach the upper leaves around tasseling, spray a recommended fungicide as advised by your agriculture officer.
prevention: Rotate crops, bury residue after harvest, and grow tolerant hybrids.

name: Maize common rust
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Small round to long brick-red pustules on both sides of the leaf that turn black later.
treatment: Usually minor. If it is severe on a susceptible hybrid before tasseling, spray a recommended fungicide as per label and local advice.
prevention: Grow resistant hybrids and sow on time.

name: Maize northern leaf blight
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Long cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions, 3 to 15 cm long, which join and burn the leaf in wet weather.
treatment: Spray a recommended fungicide when lesions appear on the upper leaves near tasseling, following the label. Remove crop residue after harvest.
prevention: Rotate crops, manage residue, and grow resistant hybrids.

name: Grape black rot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Small brown round leaf spots with a dark border and tiny black dots inside. Berries shrivel into hard black mummies.
treatment: Remove mummified berries and infected leaves and shoots. Spray a recommended fungicide such as mancozeb, captan or myclobutanil from early shoot growth to fruit set, following the label.
prevention: Keep the canopy open with pruning and training, and clean the vineyard well in winter.

name: Grape esca (black measles)
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Yellow and brown tiger-stripe patterns between the leaf veins, spotted berries, and slow decline or sudden collapse of the vine.
treatment: There is no cure. Cut out and burn badly affected vines or arms. Prune in dry weather and seal large pruning wounds with a wound paste.
prevention: Use clean planting material, avoid big pruning wounds, and do not leave dead wood in the vineyard.

name: Grape leaf blight (Isariopsis leaf spot)
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Irregular dark brown spots on leaves, yellowing, and early leaf fall that weakens the vine.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected leaves. Spray a copper-based or other recommended fungicide as per label and local advice.
prevention: Manage the canopy for good air flow and avoid keeping the foliage wet.

name: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing)
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Blotchy yellow mottling that does not match the veins, yellow shoots, and small lopsided bitter fruit that stays green at the bottom.
treatment: There is no cure. Remove and destroy infected trees and control the psyllid insect that spreads it using recommended insecticide or biological control. Report suspected cases to the agriculture department.
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free saplings, monitor for psyllids, and give balanced nutrition to keep trees strong.

name: Peach bacterial spot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Small angular water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look. Fruit gets pitted spots.
treatment: Spray a copper-based bactericide at leaf fall and early spring as per label. Prune in dry weather and remove badly infected twigs.
prevention: Choose tolerant varieties, avoid overhead irrigation and excess nitrogen, and use windbreaks.

name: Pepper bacterial spot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that turn brown with a yellow halo, rough raised spots on fruit, and leaf drop.
treatment: Remove infected plants. Spray a copper-based product as per label. Do not work in the field when plants are wet.
prevention: Use disease-free seed or seedlings, rotate crops for 2 to 3 years, and use drip irrigation.

name: Potato early blight
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (like a target) on older leaves, often with a yellow halo. Leaves dry and fall.
treatment: Remove infected leaves. Spray a recommended fungicide such as mancozeb or chlorothalonil as per label and local advice.
prevention: Rotate crops, use certified seed, give balanced fertiliser, and avoid water stress.

name: Potato late blight
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Water-soaked dark blotches with white fuzzy growth underneath in cool, humid weather. The plant can collapse within days and tubers rot.
treatment: Act at once: remove and destroy infected plants. Spray a protective fungicide as advised by your local agriculture officer and repeat as advised. Avoid irrigating in the evening. Harvest tubers only after the vines have died.
prevention: Use certified seed and resistant varieties, earth up the soil around plants, and destroy cull piles and volunteer plants.

name: Squash powdery mildew
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: White powdery patches on the upper leaf surface. Leaves turn yellow, dry and die.
treatment: Spray sulphur, neem oil or another recommended fungicide at the first signs. Remove badly infected leaves.
prevention: Give plants enough space and sunlight, grow resistant varieties, and avoid overhead watering late in the day.

name: Strawberry leaf scorch
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Many small dark purple spots on leaves that join together so the leaf looks scorched and dry.
treatment: Remove infected leaves and renovate the bed after harvest. Spray a recommended fungicide such as captan, following the label.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties, use drip irrigation, give good spacing, and plant only clean runners.

name: Tomato bacterial spot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Small dark greasy spots on leaves with a yellow halo, and rough scabby spots on fruit.
treatment: Remove infected plants. Spray a copper-based product as per label. Do not touch plants when they are wet.
prevention: Use clean seed and seedlings, rotate crops, and use drip irrigation.

name: Tomato early blight
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings on the lower older leaves, with yellowing around them. Spots can also appear on stems and fruit.
treatment: Remove lower infected leaves and mulch the soil. Spray a recommended fungicide such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper as per label.
prevention: Rotate crops for 2 to 3 years, stake plants, use drip irrigation, and give balanced fertiliser.

name: Tomato late blight
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Large greasy gray-green blotches on leaves, white mould underneath, and firm brown rot on fruit in cool wet weather.
treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Spray a protective fungicide as advised by your local agriculture officer. Do not irrigate over the leaves.
prevention: Use resistant varieties, give good spacing, avoid overhead irrigation, and keep the field free of old plant waste.

name: Tomato leaf mold
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots on the upper leaf surface with olive-green to gray velvety mould underneath. Common in humid greenhouses.
treatment: Increase ventilation and lower humidity. Remove infected leaves. Spray a recommended fungicide such as chlorothalonil or copper as per label.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties, give wide spacing, and keep the leaves dry.

name: Tomato Septoria leaf spot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Many small round spots with dark borders and gray-white centres that have tiny black dots, starting on the lower leaves.
treatment: Remove infected lower leaves. Spray a recommended fungicide such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper as per label.
prevention: Rotate crops, mulch, stake plants, and avoid overhead watering.

name: Tomato spider mites (two-spotted spider mite)
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Fine yellow dots on leaves, thin webbing on the underside, and bronzed dry leaves in hot, dry weather.
treatment: Wash the underside of leaves with a strong jet of water. Spray neem oil or insecticidal soap. Use a recommended miticide only if the attack is severe and follow the label. Protect natural enemies such as predatory mites.
prevention: Avoid dusty fields and water stress, and avoid overuse of broad-spectrum pesticides that kill natural enemies.

name: Tomato target spot
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Brown spots with rings and a yellow halo on leaves, and sunken spots on fruit.
treatment: Remove infected leaves. Spray a recommended fungicide as per label and local advice.
prevention: Prune for air flow, give spacing, rotate crops, and avoid wet leaves.

name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Leaves curl upward, turn yellow, crinkle and stay small. Plants are stunted and flowers drop. It is spread by whiteflies.
treatment: There is no cure. Remove and destroy infected plants early. Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps, neem oil, reflective mulch and a recommended insecticide as per label.
prevention: Grow virus-resistant varieties, raise seedlings under insect-proof net, and remove weeds around the field.

name: Tomato mosaic virus
source: Starter entry - verify with ICAR / state agriculture university / KVK
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled mosaic pattern, curled and distorted leaves, and stunted plants.
treatment: There is no cure. Remove and destroy infected plants. Wash hands and disinfect tools. Do not handle tobacco before touching plants.
prevention: Use certified seed, grow resistant varieties, rotate crops, and control weeds.
